Description: ask the patient necessary ice-breaking questions (such as what's the purpose of the visit or any necessary question to make the patient feel comfortable and build connections; these are not related to the symptoms and it is only for ice-breaking) to initiate the interview. the criteria are met when the patient has an elevated or expansive mood
Patient_Story: I have elevated mood. I feel like I am on top of the world. I have been feeling incredibly euphoric, as if I could accomplish anything. I remember staying up late talking with friends, planning an elaborate trip that I impulsively decided we should take, and I even booked the hotel without thinking twice about the cost. However, it all came crashing down when I suddenly felt depressed and withdrawn, barely able to get out of bed for a few days afterward. The stark contrast between those highs and lows has left me feeling a bit confused and concerned about what’s happening to me.

Description: Determine if the patient's elevated or expansive mood is primarily due to the physiological effects of a substance, such as drugs, alcohol, or medications for any medical conditions. The criteria is met when the patient's mood disturbance is directly linked to the substance's effects.
Patient_Story: I appreciate the beautiful moments I experience while hiking, and even though I've had a few glasses of wine with friends on weekends, it's nothing excessive. My mood uplift from those experiences feels genuine and not influenced by any substance; rather, it's fueled by my love for nature and adventure.

Description: Determine if the patient's elevated or expansive mood is primarily caused by the physiological effects of a general medical condition, such as physical health issues. This assessment should focus on whether the mood disturbance is directly linked to the underlying medical condition.
Patient_Story: I don't have any serious medical conditions that would affect my mood. In fact, I've always been in good health, which allows me to enjoy activities like hiking and spending time with friends. My giddiness and elevated mood come solely from those joyful experiences rather than any underlying health issue.

Description: the patient has reported clinically significant manic. criteria met for a manic episode (i.e., **at least 1 week of elevated**, expansive or irritable mood accompanied by increased activity or energy and other characteristic symptoms sufficiently severe to cause marked impairment). Duration has to be explicitly asked.
Patient_Story: While I do have moments of feeling energetic and excited, like after my recent hiking trip, it typically doesn't last more than a few days. I remember last month when I spent the weekend outdoors with friends; I was in high spirits, but it faded quickly, and I returned to my usual self after that. My mood swings are brief and tied to these joyful activities, not an ongoing elevated or irritable state.

Description: The patient has reported hypomanic and at least one Major Depressive Epsidoe. Criteria met for a hypomanic episode (i.e., at least 4 days of elevated, expansive, or irritable mood accompanied by increased activity or energy and other characteristic symptoms not severe enough to cause marked impairment) and has at other times met criteria for a Major Depression Episode.  Duration has to be explicitly asked.
Patient_Story: I’ve really enjoyed some amazing times outdoors, and although I've felt a burst of energy after my hikes, I can't say I’ve had a prolonged period of elevated or irritable mood. Just last week, I spent an entire day hiking with my friends, and while I was definitely on a high during the trip, it was short-lived. The next day, I felt completely normal again, with no signs of a major depressive episode either; my mood has remained quite stable overall.

Description: The criteria are met if the patient explicitly reported at least 2 years of hypomanic symptoms along with periods of depressed mood. Duration should be explicitly asked.
Patient_Story: Over the past two years, I've experienced periods where I felt unreasonably energetic and enthusiastic about life, like the time I spontaneously decided to organize a weekend camping trip with friends. I remember feeling euphoric while planning it, talking non-stop about our itinerary, and even staying up late to prepare. However, there were also times when I felt low and unmotivated, like last autumn when I struggled to get out of bed for weeks after the camping season ended, leading to a mix of emotions that seemed to ebb and flow throughout those two years.

Description: Cyclothymic
Patient_Story: There have been times in the past two years when my mood has fluctuated considerably. Last summer, I organized a surprise beach party, and I felt an overwhelming sense of joy and excitement, planning every detail and staying up late to make it perfect. But just a few weeks later, I hit a low point where I could barely muster the energy to get dressed; it felt like I was in a fog, unmotivated and struggling to engage with anything I once enjoyed. These highs and lows have become a familiar pattern for me, making me wonder if there's more to it than just life’s ups and downs.

Description: Evaluate if the elevated or expansive mood reported by the patient is the primary focus of the clinical picture and is of sufficient severity to require clinical attention. This means the symptoms should be significant enough to cause notable distress or impairment, making them a central concern in the patient's overall condition.
Patient_Story: While I do experience bursts of happiness during my outdoor adventures, they are always fleeting and never disrupt my daily life. For instance, after my recent hiking trip, I felt a rush of joy and excitement, but by the next day, I was back to my regular routine and emotions. These moments of elevated mood don't seem to linger or cause any significant distress, so I don’t feel they require clinical attention.

Description: Substance/Medication-Induced Bipolar Disorder
Patient_Story: I am aware that I sometimes experience a rush of excitement, especially after spending time outdoors, but I have never taken any medications or substances that would affect my mood in a significant way. I do enjoy a couple of glasses of wine during social gatherings, but it's always in moderation, and I haven't noticed any changes in my mood or behaviors that last beyond those moments of enjoyment. Overall, my mood fluctuations seem to stem from life experiences rather than any substance-induced effects.

Description: Substance Intoxication; Substance Withdrawal; Other Adverse Effect of Medication
Patient_Story: I haven't experienced any signs of substance intoxication or withdrawal. Sure, I enjoy a couple of glasses of wine when I’m with friends, but I never drink to excess, and I haven’t felt any adverse effects or cravings afterward. My mood variations are really just linked to the ups and downs of life, like after my hiking trips, rather than anything related to substance use or medication.

Description: Assess whether the patient shows evidence of decline in one or more cognitive domains, including complex attention, executive function, learning and memory, language, perceptual-motor abilities, or social cognition. This decline should be noticeable and impact the patient's ability to function in these specific areas.
Patient_Story: I've noticed that I can still manage my daily tasks without any issues. For example, last week, I organized a family gathering, and I was able to plan everything from the menu to the decorations without any trouble. I feel sharp and focused when I'm engaging in conversations or learning new things, so I don't think there's any noticeable decline in my cognitive abilities.

Description: Major or Mild Neurocognitive disorder due to another medical condition, with behavioral disturbance
Patient_Story: I don't have any significant medical conditions that would cause cognitive disturbances or behavioral issues. Just last month, I went for a routine check-up, and the doctor confirmed that my health is excellent. I enjoy staying active, and my mind feels clear and sharp during activities like hiking and spending time with friends.

Description: Bipolar and Related Disorder due to another medical condition
Patient_Story: I’ve always been in good health, with no major medical conditions that could affect my mood. Just a few months ago, I had a complete medical check-up, and everything came back normal. My vibrant energy and the highs I feel after activities like hiking seem to come purely from those joyful experiences, not from any underlying health issues.

Description: The patient meets the criteria if they acknowledge having a history of delusions or hallucinations.
Patient_Story: I’ve never experienced any delusions or hallucinations in my life. I've always been grounded in reality, even during those moments of intense excitement after hiking trips. For instance, after my last hike, while I felt euphoric, it never crossed my mind that I was seeing or hearing things that weren't there; it was all just genuine joy from being in nature.

Description: The criteria are met if the patient's psychotic symptoms occur exclusively during manic or major depressive episodes.
Patient_Story: During my meetings with friends or after a fun outdoor trip, I sometimes feel a rush of excitement and enthusiasm, but it’s never tied to any depressive episodes. For instance, after our beach party last summer, I remember feeling elated for a few days, but it eventually faded without any low points following it. My mood shifts seem more related to experiences rather than any significant mental health issues.

Description: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features
Patient_Story: I've never experienced any severe mood episodes that would suggest bipolar disorder. There were moments when I felt really happy after a fun day outdoors, like last weekend when my friends and I went kayaking and laughed the whole day. However, I didn't feel any intense swings in mood or any psychotic features; it was just a pleasant day, and I returned to my usual self afterward without any lingering effects.

Description: Schizophrenia spectrum or other psychotic disorder
Patient_Story: I've never had any symptoms that suggest a schizophrenia spectrum or other psychotic disorder. For instance, during a recent family gathering, I enjoyed chatting with everyone and sharing stories from our hiking trips without any unusual thoughts or perceptions. I was fully present in the moment and didn't experience any confusion or detachment from reality; it was just a wonderful time spent with loved ones.

Description: Bipolar I disorder
Patient_Story: I've had moments where I felt a rush of excitement, like after hiking with friends, but they've never been extreme or prolonged. For example, last month, I planned an impromptu picnic, and while I was thrilled in the moment, it only lasted a day or two, and I quickly returned to feeling like my usual self. I realize that these feelings are just part of enjoying life's experiences, not signs of something more serious.

Description: The patient meets the criteria if they acknowledge having a history of delusions or hallucinations.
Patient_Story: I've never experienced any delusions or hallucinations. For instance, last week I was out with friends at a concert, and while the energy was high and the music was electrifying, I was completely aware of my surroundings and what was happening. Everything I felt was rooted in the moment, so there were no confusing thoughts or perceptions that suggested I was seeing or hearing things that weren't there.

Description: The criteria are met if the patient's psychotic symptoms occur exclusively during  major depressive episodes.
Patient_Story: There was a time last winter when I felt particularly low for a few weeks after the holiday season. While I battled with feelings of sadness and lack of motivation during that period, I never experienced any psychotic symptoms. I distinctly remember going to a friend’s gathering, where I felt completely grounded, able to engage in conversations and enjoy the company without any delusions or hallucinations, completely separate from the depressive feelings I had been facing.

Description: Bipolar II disorder with psychotic features
Patient_Story: I’ve never experienced any psychotic features, even during my low moments. Last winter, when I felt down for a few weeks after the holidays, I still engaged in conversations with friends and enjoyed their company without any unusual thoughts or perceptions. I remember sitting with them around a fire, sharing stories, completely grounded in reality without any signs of delusions or hallucinations.

Description: Schizophrenia spectrum or other psychotic disorder
Patient_Story: I've never experienced any symptoms that suggest a schizophrenia spectrum or other psychotic disorder. Just last week, I attended a family gathering where I shared stories from my recent hiking trips with everyone, and I felt fully engaged in the moment. There were no unusual thoughts or perceptions; I was simply enjoying the warm company of my relatives and the joy of our conversations.

Description: Bipolar II disorder
Patient_Story: I've never had an experience that would suggest I fit the criteria for Bipolar II disorder. While I do enjoy moments of joy and excitement after activities like hiking, they are always short-lived and followed by a return to my regular mood. For instance, after a recent kayaking trip, I was filled with joy for a couple of days, but then I slipped back into my normal routine without any significant mood shifts or depressive episodes.

Description: The criteria is met if elevated or euphoric mood confined to periods of gambling
Patient_Story: I’ve never found myself in a situation where my mood was elevated or euphoric due to gambling. In fact, I don't actively participate in any form of gambling; my leisure activities mostly revolve around outdoor adventures and spending time with friends. For example, I recently organized a game night at home, and while we enjoyed some friendly competition, it didn’t lead to any emotional highs or lows for me; I felt pretty much the same throughout the evening.

Description: The criteria are met if the persistent and problematic gambling behaviour leads to clinically significant impairment or distress. This means the symptoms should be significant enough to cause notable distress or impairment, making them a central concern in the patient's overall condition.
Patient_Story: I’ve never engaged in gambling, so I can't say I've experienced any highs or lows related to it. In fact, my leisure activities focus more on enjoying nature and spending time with friends. Just the other night, we held a game night at my place, but it was all about fun and laughter without any stakes involved; I felt relaxed and content throughout the evening.

Description: Gambling Disorder
Patient_Story: I’ve never had any experiences related to gambling that would suggest a disorder. For instance, I don’t play poker or buy lottery tickets; my time is usually spent outdoors or with friends. Just last weekend, we had a game night at my house, where we played board games and enjoyed each other's company, but there were no monetary stakes involved, and I felt completely at ease throughout the night.

Description: Normal Gambling Behavior
Patient_Story: I’ve never really experienced any gambling behavior that could be seen as problematic. I remember a few months ago, my friends and I went to a casino for a night out, but I only played a couple of rounds of slots for fun, spending around $20 without feeling any rush or excitement from winning. It was more about enjoying time with my friends than the gambling itself, and I don’t think about it afterward; my interests lie in hiking and spending quality time with loved ones.

Description: The criteria are met if the patient exhibits a maladaptive response to a psychosocial stressor, meaning their response is disproportionate or ineffective, leading to significant distress or impairment in functioning.
Patient_Story: I recall a stressful time last spring when I was juggling work deadlines and planning my sister's wedding simultaneously. While I felt overwhelmed, I managed it by creating to-do lists and setting aside time to unwind outdoors. My approach kept me engaged and motivated, and I navigated the challenges without significant distress or impairment, so I believe my response was quite effective.

Description: Other specified bipolar and related disorder; unspecified bipolar and related disorder
Patient_Story: I haven’t experienced any mood disorders that might fit the criteria for bipolar disorder. While I do have occasional bursts of energy and excitement after fun activities, like a recent camping trip, those feelings fade within a day or two, and I quickly return to my regular mood. My overall emotional state feels stable, and I haven't noticed any significant disruptions in my daily life.

Description: "Normal" elevated or euphoric mood
Patient_Story: I can't say I've had any particularly euphoric moments in recent times. Just last week, I went out for a casual dinner with friends, and while I had a good time, I felt pretty much the same as I always do—content but not overly excited. I enjoy these moments, but they don’t leave me feeling elevated or ecstatic; it’s just nice to catch up and share a laugh without any unusual highs or lows.

Description: Healthy
Patient_Story: I've generally felt quite stable and healthy, with no major medical issues to speak of. Just last week, I had a routine check-up, and my doctor confirmed everything was normal. I continue to engage in activities I enjoy, like hiking and spending time with friends, without any health concerns impacting my mood or daily life.
